newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Russian unemployment sparks suicide, crime-report.
newsitem.headline: Russian unemployment sparks suicide, crime-report.

text.p: Surging unemployment in Russia, far higher than official figures suggest, has sparked a sharp rise in suicides and a doubling of the crime rate, according to a new report released on Wednesday.

The report, by International Labour Organisation (ILO) expert Guy Standing, and a book he is also publishing this week, takes issue with economists who say Russia is emerging from slump and contends the country is still in deep upheaval.

"For the past five years, unemployment in Russia has been chronically understated and is well over 10 per cent," says the report, based on a labour survey carried out by an ILO team led by Standing since the early 1990s.

Official statistics, often cited by Western economists who have worked with the Russian government as an illustration of the success of reform, have consistently put unemployment in the 1990s at from one to 2.5 per cent.
The total Russian workforce is estimated at approximately 70 million.

Standing's book, "Russian Unemployment and Enterprise Restructuring," suggests much of the deterioration in the labour market is due to an unprecedented decline in life expectancy and disappearance of people normally counted as employed.
It is being launched this week in London and New York.

With a sub-title "Reviving Dead Souls", a reference to 19th century Russian novel by Nikolai Gogol in which landowners traded serfs whose deaths have been unregistered to avoid loss of tax relief, the book argues a similar situation exists today.

According to official data, it says, the death rates of young and middle-aged men -- who would be expected to be on the job market or registered with labour exchanges -- rose sharply between 1990 and 1994.

In his report, to be delivered as a lecture in London on Wednesday, Standing voices conviction that real unemployment and even official figures would be much higher if workers, especially men, had not disappeared "through premature death."
Since the late 1980s and the 1991 collapse of the Soviet communist system, he says, average life expectancy in Russia has declined by over five years -- from 65 in 1987 to 58 in 1995 among males.
"While declining public health care has played a part in the rising mortality, it seems that economic insecurity and stress have been the main factors," the report declares.

Standing says the number of working-age people dying from alcoholism, a form of escape from stress caused by joblessness, more than tripled between 1990 and 1995, while the number of murders more than doubled and suicides went up 1.6 times.
"The growth in suicide is extraordinary," he declares, adding that it is increasingly concentrated among young and middle-aged men, although also rising sharply among women.
Overall, suicide and death among working-age people "seem disproportionately concentrated among the jobless," he says.

While total crime and the number of criminal convictions has more than doubled in the 1990s, he adds, the percentage of all those convicted who were out of work also more than doubled and accounted for 44 per cent of the total in 1995.
As a result, the ILO expert argues, many people who might otherwise have been counted among the unemployed are in jail.
